seo.title: Rear Camera vs Front Camera for Passport and Visa Photos | FlyFrame
seo.description: Rear or front camera for a passport or visa photo? Compare resolution, distance, distortion, framing and settings, with the distances and steps for each.

hero.title: Rear Camera vs Front Camera for Passport and Visa Photos
hero.intro: Both cameras on your phone can take a passport or visa photo, but they work differently. This guide is for anyone taking their own photo at home. It compares the two cameras, explains how distance changes the look of a face, and gives the settings and distances to use with each.

image.alt: Two portraits of the same woman: a rear camera photo, labelled sharper and clearer, and a front camera photo, labelled easier to frame your face

sections.title: Rear camera vs front camera: Which is better for passport and visa photos?

blocks.text: Both front and rear cameras can be used to take passport and visa photos, but each has its advantages. The rear camera generally offers better image quality, while the front camera makes it easier to frame yourself and check your position before capturing.

In the rear camera had a higher resolution than the front camera. However, it doesn't provide a live preview of your face while shooting, so you may need someone to help, or [use a phone stand and timer](/guide/take-a-passport-photo-alone) to capture the photo.

The front camera, on the other hand, lets you see yourself on the screen while taking the picture. This makes positioning easier, especially when you're taking the photo yourself. However, holding the phone too close can [distort facial proportions](#facial-distortion).
Getting the distance right
**Distance matters more than which camera you choose.** When the camera is too close to your face, facial features can appear distorted, affecting how your face looks in the final image.
As a practical starting point:

items: **Rear camera:** Position your phone approximately 1–2 metres (4–6 feet) away. Use a stand or ask someone to help you frame the shot.
**Front camera:** Hold your phone approximately 40–50 cm (16–20 inches) away, while keeping your face centred and avoiding extreme close-ups.

blocks.text: With either camera, use the [standard 1x lens](#settings), turn off the flash, portrait mode and beauty filters, and keep the original photo without applying edits.

sections.title: What a passport or visa photo needs from the camera

blocks.text: Now that you know which camera to use and how to position it, the next step is making sure the camera captures a photo with the right quality.

Regardless of whether you choose the front or rear camera, your passport or visa photo should be **sharp, clear and evenly lit**, with your **whole face visible and its natural proportions maintained**.
Focus on these three important aspects when capturing your photo:

items: **Sharpness:** Your face should be clearly focused, without [blur, excessive noise or loss of detail](/guide/fix-a-blurry-passport-photo).
**Lighting:** Your face should be evenly illuminated, without [harsh shadows](/guide/avoid-shadows-in-passport-photos), glare or overexposure.
**Natural appearance:** Your facial features should remain true to life. Avoid [beauty filters, portrait effects](/guide/filters-and-portrait-mode) or digital enhancements that alter your appearance.

dont.alt: Don't: the same portrait out of focus and blurred

do.alt: Do: a sharp, clearly focused portrait

dont.alt: Don't: the same portrait with a harsh shadow over one side of the face and glare on the other

do.alt: Do: a portrait with the face evenly lit

dont.alt: Don't: the same portrait with a beauty filter that smooths the skin, tints it pink and slims the face

blocks.text: The camera you use helps determine the quality of the image, but how you position yourself, [the lighting around you](/guide/lighting-for-passport-photos) and the way you capture the photo matter just as much.
The goal is to produce a clear, natural-looking photograph that accurately represents your face and is suitable for your [passport or visa application](/guide/photo-requirements-by-country).

sections.title: Rear camera vs front camera in detail

blocks.text: The table above lists the differences. Here is what each one changes in the photo you upload, with the rear camera and with the front camera.
Resolution

Resolution decides how much detail your photo still holds once the editor crops it to [your country's size](/guide/passport-photo-sizes-by-country), and how far it can be enlarged or printed before it looks soft.

items: **Rear camera:** The photo starts with more pixels, so after it is cropped to a passport size your face keeps plenty of detail. Your hairline, eyebrows and the outline of your face stay crisp, even when the photo is printed.

items.text: **Front camera:** The photo starts with fewer pixels. That is usually still enough for a passport-size photo, but there is less detail to spare once it is cropped, so any blur or grain shows more and the photo can look softer when printed.
items.fix: You can still get a sharp, detailed photo with it. Set the camera to its highest resolution, use the 1x lens and give it soft, even light, and the photo will stay sharp after it is cropped.

image.alt: Rear camera: a portrait with more pixels, smooth and sharp
Front camera: the same portrait with fewer pixels, shown as visible blocks

blocks.text: Aperture
The aperture decides how much light reaches the camera. In the photo, it shows in how bright and clean your face looks, especially indoors.

items: **Rear camera:** More light comes in, so the photo is brighter and cleaner, with even skin tones and little grain in the darker areas. The camera can also take the photo faster, so a small movement is less likely to blur it.

items.text: **Front camera:** Less light comes in. In a dim room the photo can look darker or grainy, or the phone brightens it with processing that smooths away fine detail.
items.fix: This is easy to make up for. Take the photo in daylight, facing a window or another [soft light source](/guide/lighting-for-passport-photos), and the camera will have plenty of light without needing to brighten the photo.

image.alt: Rear camera: a bright, clean portrait taken with more light
Front camera: the same portrait darker and grainier, taken with less light

blocks.text: Examples of current phone cameras
These are the manufacturers' published specifications for two current phones. Specifications differ by model, so check yours in your phone's settings or on the manufacturer's page.

In both examples the rear camera has more megapixels and a wider aperture. A lower ƒ-number means a wider aperture, which lets in more light. Both front cameras here have autofocus, so a front camera can still give a sharp photo.
Preview while shooting
The preview decides how well your face is placed in the photo: centred, straight, and with your whole head and shoulders in the frame.

items.text: **Rear camera:** You can't see yourself while you shoot, so the first photos are often off-centre or too tight, with the top of your head or your shoulders cut off. It usually takes a helper or a few test shots to get the framing right.
items.fix: A helper sorts this straight away. On your own, put the phone on a stand with the timer on, take a test photo and check it, then take the final one.

items.text: **Front camera:** You can see your face as you shoot, so it is easier to centre your head and leave space around it. If you look at the screen instead of the lens, though, your eyes can look slightly down in the photo.
items.fix: Just look at the camera lens, the small circle at the top of the phone, while the photo is taken, and your eyes will look straight ahead.

image.alt: Rear camera, without a preview: a portrait off-centre with the top of the head cut off
Front camera, with a preview: the same portrait centred inside a face guide and framing corners

blocks.text: Facial distortion

This is the difference you are most likely to notice, because it changes the shape of your face in the photo. A study in JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery (Paskhover and Fried, 2018) compared a selfie taken about 12 inches (30 cm) from the face with a photo taken at 5 feet (1.5 m). At 12 inches:

items.label: wider at the base of the nose

items: **Rear camera:** Taken from a metre or more away, your face keeps its natural proportions. Your nose, cheeks and ears look the way they do in person, so the photo looks like you.

items.text: **Front camera:** Taken from arm's length, the parts of your face closest to the lens look larger. Your nose can look wider and your face rounder, while your ears look smaller or disappear behind your cheeks. Some of this remains even at the recommended 40 to 50 cm.
items.fix: A few small changes keep your face looking natural. Hold the phone at the longer end of 40 to 50 cm, at eye level, with the 1x lens rather than the ultra-wide one. Propping it on a stand and stepping back, or switching to the rear camera, reduces the effect even more.

image.alt: Rear camera: a portrait with natural facial proportions
Front camera: an illustration of the same face taken too close, with the nose and the middle of the face enlarged

blocks.text: Typical shooting distance

Distance decides how much of you is in the photo, and how much room the editor has to crop it to your country's head size and position. The exact distances are in [Which distance to use with each camera](#distance) below.

items: **Rear camera:** From 1–2 metres, your head and shoulders sit in the frame with space around them, so the editor can crop the photo without cutting anything off.

items.text: **Front camera:** From arm's length, your face fills most of the frame. There is less space around your head, so your hair or chin can end up too close to the edge, and the editor has less room to crop.
items.fix: Hold the phone a little further away, or prop it on a stand, and check on the screen that there is space above your head and around your shoulders. Leave the cropping to the editor.

image.alt: Rear camera: a head-and-shoulders portrait taken from further away, with space around the head
Front camera: the same face close up, filling the frame

blocks.text: Image detail
Detail is what makes the photo look sharp when you zoom in on your eyes, eyebrows and hair, and it is what a photo check looks at when it judges sharpness.

items: **Rear camera:** Fine details such as eyelashes, single hairs and the edges of your eyes come out clearly, so the photo stays sharp after it is cropped, resized or printed.

items.text: **Front camera:** Fine details can look smoother or slightly smudged, because on many phones the front camera has smaller hardware and the phone smooths the photo more. In good light the difference is small; in dim light it shows more.
items.fix: With a clean lens and good light, the front camera can still take a sharp photo. Tap to focus on your face, turn off beauty mode, then zoom in on the photo to check that your eyes are sharp.

image.alt: Rear camera: a close view of the woman's face with fine detail in her eyelashes, eyebrows and hair
Front camera: the same close view with the fine detail in her eyelashes, eyebrows and hair smoothed away

blocks.text: Self-capture convenience
How you hold the phone when you are on your own shows in how straight and steady the photo comes out.

items: **Rear camera:** It takes more setup, but once the phone is on a stand at eye level with [the timer on](/guide/take-a-passport-photo-alone), the photo comes out straight and steady.

items.text: **Front camera:** It is quick to take on your own, but a phone held in your hand often tilts or moves slightly, which shows as a tilted head or a little blur.
items.fix: Prop the phone on a stand, or against something steady at eye level, and use the timer, and the photo will come out straight and sharp.

image.alt: Rear camera, on a stand: a straight, sharp portrait
Front camera, held in the hand: the same portrait slightly tilted and blurred by movement

sections.title: Which distance to use with each camera

blocks.text: These [distances](/guide/camera-distance-for-passport-photos) are our guidance for getting a clean photo. They are not rules set by any country.

image.alt: A man standing side-on to a phone on a tripod, with the gap between his face and the phone marked as 40 to 50 cm
Rear camera: a woman standing side-on to a phone on a tripod 1 to 2 metres (4 to 6 feet) away
Front camera: the same woman with the phone on a tripod 40 to 50 cm (16 to 20 inches) away

items.label: Rear camera
items.text: Use a stand, a tripod or a helper. Leave space above your head and around your shoulders.

items.label: Front camera
items.text: Keep your arm steady, or prop the phone on a stand. Hold the camera at the longer end of the range.

blocks.text: Whatever the distance, **don't zoom in** with the camera. Stand further back instead and leave space around your head and shoulders. You don't need to crop the photo yourself, because [the editor](/drop) crops it to [your country's size](/guide/passport-photo-sizes-by-country).

rows.label: Lens
rows.text: Use the standard 1x main lens, not ultra-wide and not telephoto

rows.label: Resolution
rows.text: Choose the highest photo resolution available

rows.label: Flash
rows.text: It can cause glare on skin and [glasses](/guide/glasses-in-passport-photos), and [red eyes](/guide/red-eye-in-passport-photos)

rows.label: Beauty and skin-smoothing effects
rows.text: The photo should show how you really look

rows.label: Grid
rows.text: So you can keep the camera level

rows.label: Timer
rows.text: For 3 to 10 seconds, so the phone doesn't shake when you press the button

rows.label: Focus
rows.text: Tap on your face if the phone lets you, so the face is the sharpest part

sections.title: How to take the photo with the rear camera

image.alt: A helper photographing a woman against a light blue wall with a phone's rear camera. Marked with a tick: the phone close enough that her head and shoulders fill the screen. Marked with a cross: the phone too far away, so she looks small on the screen.

items: Open [your country's rules](/guide/photo-requirements-by-country) in our hub, so you know the size, background and expression rules.
Put the phone on a **stand or tripod**, or ask a helper to hold it, with the camera at your **eye level**.

Stand **about 1 to 2 metres** (4 to 6 feet) from the phone, in front of a [plain wall](/guide/passport-photo-background-rules), and a little away from the wall so there is [no shadow](/guide/avoid-shadows-in-passport-photos).
Face a **window** or another [soft light source](/guide/lighting-for-passport-photos), so your face is evenly lit.
Set the **timer**, look straight at the camera lens, keep your eyes open, your mouth closed, and your [expression neutral](/guide/appearance-and-facial-expression).
Take **at least five photos**, and open each one at full size to pick the sharpest.

sections.title: How to take the photo with the front camera

image.alt: A woman taking a selfie against a light blue wall. Marked with a tick: the phone at eye level and at arm's length, so her face looks natural. Marked with a cross: the phone held close and below her face, so her chin and nose look larger.

items: Open [your country's rules](/guide/photo-requirements-by-country) in our hub, and turn off **beauty mode, portrait mode, filters and flash**.
Stand in front of a **plain wall**, a little away from it, and face a window or another soft light source.
Prop the phone on a stand if you can. If you hold it, hold it at **eye level** and **about 40 to 50 cm** (16 to 20 inches) from your face, with your arm as steady as possible.
**Look at the camera lens, not at the screen.** The lens is the small circle on the front of the phone.
Check on the screen that your [whole head](/guide/head-position-and-size) is in the frame, with space above it and around your shoulders.
Use the **timer**, keep your head level, eyes open, mouth closed, and expression neutral.
Take **at least five photos**, and open each one at full size to pick the sharpest.

sections.title: After the photo: what to check

image.alt: Eight photos of the same woman on a light blue background. One is sharp, evenly lit and well framed, marked with a tick. The others are marked with a cross for common problems: blur, a shadow behind the head, glare on glasses, the camera too close or too far away, and low resolution.

items.label: Sharpness
items.text: Zoom in on your eyes. They should be in focus, not [blurry or grainy](/guide/fix-a-blurry-passport-photo).

items.label: Light
items.text: No [shadows](/guide/avoid-shadows-in-passport-photos) on your face or the wall, and no glare on your skin or glasses.

items.label: Shape
items.text: Your face looks natural, with the nose not exaggerated. If it looks stretched, take the photo again from further away.

items.label: Position
items.text: Your head and the camera are level, and your whole head is in the frame.

items.label: File
items.text: You have the original photo, not a screenshot, and not a copy sent through a chat app, because [compressing a photo](/guide/passport-photo-file-size-and-format) removes detail.

Turn them off before shooting

sections.title: Can one photo work for both passport and visa?

blocks.text: **The camera advice is the same for both.** Passport and visa photo requirements can vary depending on the country and application type: a visa photo can have a different size, background colour or file-size limit for online uploads. Check the rule for your destination on our [visa photo requirements by country](/guide/visa-photo-requirements-by-country) page.
You can easily adjust your photo to meet the required specifications using our [Passport & Visa Photo Editor](/drop).
Want to understand the differences and similarities? Read our [Passport vs Visa Photo Guide](/guide/passport-vs-visa-photos).

items.q: Which camera is better for a passport photo?
items.a: No official guidance we reviewed requires a particular camera. What matters is that the photo meets your country's requirements. In the two phones we checked, the rear camera has a higher resolution, and it is shot from further away. The front camera lets you check your framing.

items.q: Can I use the front camera?
items.a: Yes, if the photo meets your country's requirements. Hold the camera at about 40 to 50 cm, at eye level, look at the lens and turn off beauty mode, portrait mode and filters.

items.q: Why does my face look different in selfies?
items.a: Because of the shooting distance. A study found that a selfie taken at about 12 inches made the base of the nose appear about 30 percent wider than a photo taken at 5 feet. Shooting from further away reduces this.

items.q: Does the number of megapixels matter?
items.a: A higher-resolution original keeps more detail after the photo is cropped to your country's size. Choose the highest photo resolution on your phone, and upload the original file.

items.q: Should I ask someone to take the photo?
items.a: Official passport guidance we reviewed mentions having another person take the photo. A helper makes it easier to use the rear camera at the right distance, but a stand or timer works too.
